notes.text: A season — A certain time appointed by God for its being and continuance, which no human wit or providence can alter. And by virtue of this appointment of God, all vicissitudes which happen in the world, whether comforts or calamities, come to pass. Which is here added to prove the principal proposition, That all things below are vain, and happiness is not to be found in them, because of their great uncertainty, and mutability, and transitoriness, and because they are so much out of the reach and power of men, and wholly in the disposal of God. Purpose - Not only natural, but even the voluntary actions of men, are ordered and disposed by God. But it must be considered, that he does not here speak of a time allowed by God, wherein all the following things may lawfully be done, but only of a time fixed by God, in which they are actually done.
To die — And as there is a time to die, so there is a time to rise again, a set time when they that lie in the grave shall be remembered.
To kill — When men die a violent death. To heal - When he who seemed to be mortally wounded is healed.
To weep — When men have just occasion for weeping.
Stones — Which were brought together in order to the building of a wall or house. To embrace - When persons perform all friendly offices one to another.

To life — When men lose their estates, either by God's providence, or by their own choice. To cast away - When a man casts away his goods voluntarily, as in a storm, to save his life, or out of love and obedience to God.
To rent — When men rend their garments, as they did in great and sudden griefs.
To love — When God stirs up love, or gives occasion for the exercise of it.

What profit — Seeing then all events are out of man's power, and no man can do or enjoy any thing at his pleasure, but only when God pleaseth, as has been shewed in many particulars, and is as true and certain in all others, hence it follows, that all men's labours, without God's blessing, are unprofitable, and utterly insufficient to make them happy.

Seen — I have diligently observed mens various employments, and the different successes of them. Hath given - Which God hath imposed upon men as their duty; to which therefore men ought quickly to submit. Exercised - That hereby they might have constant matter of exercise for their diligence, and patience, and submission to God's will and providence.

He hath — This seems to be added as at apology for God's providence, notwithstanding all the contrary events and confusions which are in the world. He hath made (or doth make or do, by his providence in the government of the world) every thing (which he doth either immediately, or by the ministry of men, or other creatures) beautiful (convenient, so that, all things considered, it could not have been done better) in its time or station, (when it was most fit to be done). Many events seem to mens shallow judgments, to be very irregular and unbecoming, as when wicked men prosper, and good men are oppressed; but when men shall throughly understand God's works, and the whole frame and contexture of them, and see the end of them, they will say, all things were done wisely. He hath set - It is true, God hath put the world into mens hearts, or made them capable of observing all the dispensations of God in the world; but this is to be understood with a limitation, because there are some more mysterious works of God, which no man can fully, understand, because he cannot search them out from the beginning to the end.
Them — In creatures or worldly enjoyments. To do good - To employ them in acts of charity and liberality.
Should eat — Use what God hath given him.

glossa.text: *All things have their time.* ((HIER.)) Above he taught the uncertain and fluctuating state of the human condition, etc., *as far as* they are contained neither by place nor by time.
*A time to plant,* etc. ((ID.)) It is doubtful to none, etc., *as far as* because perfect charity casteth out fear.

*A time to destroy,* etc. We cannot build up good things, unless we have first destroyed the evil ones, as it was said to Jeremias by God, that he should first root up and dig under and destroy, and afterwards build and plant ((Jerem. I)).

*A time to mourn,* etc. We must mourn now, that in the time to come we may dance that dance which David [danced] before the ark of the testament ((II Reg. VI)). Displeasing to the daughter of Saul, he pleased God the more.

*A time to scatter stones,* etc. ((HIER.)) I wonder, etc., *as far as* and calls to penance.

*A time to embrace.* A time to embrace wisdom, and to cleave more strictly to contemplation; and a time to be made far from the embrace, namely of wisdom, that we may serve the care of the time, and those things without which we cannot live.

*A time to keep silence, and a time.* ((HIER.)) We teach in the churches what we do not know. We do not learn any of the arts without a teacher, this alone is so cheap and so easy that it does not need a master. Nothing seems to us to be right, save what we learn, so that after much silence we may be made masters out of disciples.

 *A time to speak.* The discipline of Pythagoras is to keep silence for five years, and afterwards, being learned, to speak.

*A time of love.* A time of loving, after God, wives, children, kinsfolk, and a time of hating them, in martyrdom. Or, *Because now we see through a glass in a dark manner ((I Cor. XIII))*, etc. There will be a time of loving the presence of God, and a time of hating, when, beholding face to face and advancing unto better things, we shall begin to hate and to despise what we have loved.

*A time of war.* Now, for those not doing penance; a time of peace in the time to come, when all Israel shall be saved; *A time of war,* be not secure, take the armour of God.
*I have seen the affliction which he gave,* etc. ((HIER.)) It is said that God therefore, etc., *as far as* he made them to grow, to remain and to be changed even to the end of the age.
*And I have known.* ((HIERON.)) Therefore man was set as a husbandman in the world, etc., *as far as* hence:

*Every man that eateth and drinketh,* etc., For many now are the tribulations of the just, but in the time to come there shall be no labour in Jacob.

*I have learned,* etc. ((ID.)) There is nothing new in the world, the course of the sun, the changes of the moon, the dryness of the earth and of the trees, or their greenness, were founded together with the world; and these things God therefore tempered by a fixed reckoning, that we might understand the Providence of God in them, and might fear before the face of God. But the countenance of the Lord is upon them that do evil things.

notes.text: In — Not only in Israel, but among all nations. Which shews that this psalm speaks of the Messiah, and the times of the New Testament. Heavens - Where thy throne of glory is established, where the blessed angels celebrate thy praises, where Christ sitteth at thy right hand in glorious majesty, from whence he poureth down excellent gifts upon babes.

Babes — Weak and foolish, and contemptible persons, who are frequently called babes or children. Such are very unfit to grapple with an enemy: and therefore when such persons conquer the most powerful and malicious enemies, it must needs confound them, and advance the glory of God: as indeed it did, when such mean persons as the apostles, and disciples of Christ, maintained and propagated the gospel, in spite of all the wit, power, and rage of their enemies. Ordained - Perfectly or firmly settled strength; that is, the praise of his strength or power, Matt. xxi, 16, it is rendered praise. Still - Silence and confound them. Avenger - The devil, and all who are his vassals and espouse his quarrel.

The moon — Either the sun is included under this general title: or he omitted it, because he made this psalm by night. Ordained - Placed in that excellent and unalterable order, and directed to their several motions.

What is man — How mean and inconsiderable a thing is man, if compared with thy glorious majesty. Man - Hebrew. infirm, or miserable man. By which it is apparent that he speaks of man, not according to the state of his creation, but as fallen into a state of sin and misery, and mortality. Mindful - Carest for him, and conferest such high favours upon him. The son - Hebrew. the son of Adam, that great apostate from God, the sinful son of a sinful father, his son by likeness of disposition and manners, no less than by procreation. All which tends to magnify the following mercy. Visitest - Not in anger, as that word is sometimes used, but with thy grace and mercy.

For — Thou hast in Christ mercifully restored man to his primitive estate, wherein he was but one remove below the angels; from which he was fallen by sin. Crowned - Man, fallen and lost man: who is actually restored to glory and dominion in Christ his head and representative, who received this crown and dominion for man's good, and in his stead; which he will in due time communicate to his members. And so the two expositions of this place concerning mankind and concerning Christ, may be reconciled. For he speaks of that honourable estate conferred first upon Christ, and then by his hands upon mankind. But the words more literally rendered are, Thou madest him a little less than God. And hence some have inferred, that man in his original state was the highest of all creatures. David praises God for giving him victory over his enemies, ver. 1-6. Triumphs in confidence that God would judge the world and protect his people, ver. 7-10. Calls others to praise him, ver. 11, 12. Prays for help, and praises God, ver. 13-20. To the chief musician upon Muth-labben, A psalm of David Title of the psalm. Muth-labben - This also seems to be a title of some tune, or instrument: of which we may be content to be ignorant, as the Jewish doctors are.

glossa.text: « O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name! etc. » ((CASS.)) First the praises of God, his majesty, and his exalted working are described. « In the whole. » ((Ibid.)) Let not the Jews therefore, or any others, claim for themselves what belongs to all, which is the intent. « Above the heavens. » ((AUG.)) Literally, or the Scriptures: because it exceeds the utterances of all the Scriptures; or, « above the heavens. » Continuing with what follows, that is, into the Scriptures, which he bends down to babes, on account of the enemies of the cross: who are destroyed, when the Scriptures are seen, that is, understood, to be led down as far as babes: and when through them they are nourished unto strength, and are raised to the sublimity of understanding.

« Out of the mouth of infants. » ((Ibid.)) Of the unwise, to whom the Apostle gave milk, whom those signified who praised the Lord, in whom the Lord uses this testimony. Out of these he hath perfected praise, because if only the perfect were in the Church, no counsel would be taken for the human race; as now, when even the least, not yet capable of the knowledge of spiritual things, are nourished by faith in the history of things temporal. « Enemies » are all who speak things contrary to the dispensation made through the Crucified. « Defenders » the heretics seem of the faith, the philosophers of wisdom, although yet the former impugn the faith, and the latter true wisdom. « Sucklings, » ((CASS.)) not in age, but as Peter has it, « as newborn babes ((I Petr. II)), » who cannot yet take food, but milk; and it is: thou art proclaimed not only by the perfect, but also by the unwise. Or, he calls infants and sucklings the apostles, who were simple and unlearned men; whence: « The foolish things of the world « God hath chosen, that he may confound the strong ((I Cor. I)). » The praise is more perfect. Or, out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, that is, out of the words of the Hebrew children thou hast perfected praise, which seemed to be done childishly, on account of the enemies, that it might not seem to be human wisdom, but divinely given. « Thine enemies. » The pagans. « The enemy. » The Jew, who is an enemy of God, while he defends the Father alone: because « he that honoureth not the Son, honoureth not « the Father, » or an enemy in his will.

« For I shall see. » Before the Jew, in spirit. « Thy heavens, » the apostles, I shall see present in their descendants; this well suits those of the first age. « The works of thy fingers. » Because they are perfected by the cooperation of the Trinity, which is signified here in the three fingers, as there: « Who weigheth the bulk of the earth with three fingers. » ((Isa. XL.)) And through them, « The moon and the stars which thou hast founded. » Not they.

« What is man. » ((Ibid.)) Secondly, he says that the nature of man, once corrupted, is exalted in Christ above all things. For before he had shown the omnipotence of the Godhead. By man, sinners; by the son of man, the spiritual. ((Ibid.)) Man, any vile person, of whom God is mindful in showing mercy, the Son of man, Christ as man: since through him thou visitest him, when the Word was made flesh, in which the physician came to the sick. « Or the son. » ((AUG.)) The disjunction hints that there is a distance between man and the son of man. Every son of man is man, but not conversely, as Adam. Every man therefore, who bears the image of the earthly: the Son of man, who is heavenly, and deservedly a new man, son of man: because the new is made out of the old by a certain change. ((AUG.)) Why, leaving the higher things, does he speak of these lowest ones? But the sheep, etc., *as far as* who by the seed of the word of God make the hearts of men to bear fruit.

« Moreover the cattle also. » He notes therefore that the wicked also are subject to Christ, which seems less: for these carnal men dwell in the breadth of the plain, that is, in the amplitude of pleasures, not in the mountains of virtues. « The cattle of the field. » ((Ibid.)) Who live in the flesh, where they climb nothing steep: but the broad way, to which they cling, is that which leads to destruction: whence also Abel is slain in the field.

« The birds, » the proud: of whom, « They have set their mouth against heaven ((Psal. LXXII)). » Whose head says: « I will ascend into heaven, and I will exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High ((Isa. XIV)). « The fishes of the sea that walk through the paths of the sea, » the curious. These three, the pleasure of the flesh, pride, curiosity, include all vices, which are the concupiscence of the flesh, the ambition of the world, that is, pride, the concupiscence of the eyes, since through the eyes curiosity chiefly prevails.

notes.text: And I saw — So it runs, chap. xix, 11, xx, 1, 4, 11, in a succession. All these several representations follow one another in order: so the vision reaches into eternity. A new heaven and a new earth - After the resurrection and general judgment. St. John is not now describing a flourishing state of the church, but a new and eternal state of all things. For the first heaven and the first earth - Not only the lowest part of heaven, not only the solar system, but the whole ethereal heaven, with all its host, whether of planets or fixed stars, Isai xxxiv, 4 Matt. xxiv, 29. All the former things will be done away, that all may become new, verses 4, 5, 2 Pet. iii, 10, 12. Are passed away - But in the fourth verse it is said, "are gone away." There the stronger word is used; for death, mourning, and sorrow go away all together: the former heaven and earth only pass away, giving place to the new heaven and the new earth.

And I saw the holy city — The new heaven, the new earth, and the new Jerusalem, are closely connected. This city is wholly new, belonging not to this world, not to the millennium, but to eternity. This appears from the series of the vision, the magnificence of the description, and the opposition of this city to the second death, chap. xx, 11, 12; xxi, 1, 2, 5, 8, 9; xxii, 5. Coming down - In the very act of descending.
They shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God — So shall the covenant between God and his people be executed in the most glorious manner.

And death shall be no more — This is a full proof that this whole description belongs not to time, but eternity. Neither shall sorrow, or crying, or pain, be any more: for the former things are gone away - Under the former heaven, and upon the former earth, there was death and sorrow, crying and pain; all which occasioned many tears: but now pain and sorrow are fled away, and the saints have everlasting life and joy.

And he that sat upon the throne said — Not to St. John only. From the first mention of "him that sat upon the throne," chap. iv, 2, this is the first speech which is expressly ascribed to him. And he - The angel. Saith to me Write - As follows. These sayings are faithful and true - This includes all that went before. The apostle seems again to have ceased writing, being overcome with ecstasy at the voice of him that spake.

And he — That sat upon the throne. Said to me, It is done - All that the prophets had spoken; all that was spoken, chap. iv, 1. We read this expression twice in this prophecy: first, chap. xvi, 17, at the fulfilling of the wrath of God; and here, at the making all things new. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end - The latter explains the former: the Everlasting. I will give to him that thirsteth - The Lamb saith the same, chap. xxii, 17.

glossa.text: *And I saw.* In this seventh vision he treats of the renewing of the elements and the glorification of the saints, describing the merits through which the saints are thus glorified. *A new heaven and a new earth.* The change of the air and of the earth is not doubtful, but that it comes to pass through fire. But concerning water there is doubt, for it is believed to have purgation in itself.

*As a bride adorned.* As a bridegroom sends gifts beforehand to his bride before he leads her home, so does Christ send to the Church faith and virtues and good works before he receives her into glory.

*A great voice from the throne.* When he had said that he had seen the renewing of the elements and the glorification of the saints, this was unknown, and, lest it should seem past believing, he adds the authority of the holy Fathers, who foretold this. *Behold the tabernacle.* That is, it is plain that the humanity of Christ shall be in that same glory in which it warred, and the men who imitated him and used those things well.

 *And they his people.* That is, offending in nothing, which cannot be while they are in mortal flesh.
*And death.* Truly there shall be no tears there, because there shall be no cause of tears.

*And he said.* As if he should say: Write whatsoever has been shown thee concerning this renewing. This was done for the profit of those now present, for whom I have been bidden to write these things. *Write: for these,* etc. Bidding him write, and announce to others, he subjoins an exhortation, that all may labour to belong to this renewing.

*And he said to me.* When the authority of the saints concerning this renewing has been set down, he sets down the authority of God himself. *It is done.* Lest anyone should ask: What shall come to pass after that renewing, it is said to him that nothing remains to be done.

 *Alpha and Omega.* As if he should say: This renewing I shall be able to make, because I created all things, and in me all things shall be consummated. *To him that thirsteth.* I will give, not to him that thirsteth for an hour, but to him that perseveres.

notes.text: Inherit the kingdom — Purchased by my blood, for all who have believed in me with the faith which wrought by love. Prepared for you - On purpose for you. May it not be probably inferred from hence, that man was not created merely to fill up the places of the fallen angels?

I was hungry, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink — All these works of outward mercy suppose faith and love, and must needs he accompanied with works of spiritual mercy. But works of this kind the Judge could not mention in the same manner. He could not say, I was in error, and ye recalled me to the truth; I was in sin, and ye brought me to repentance. In prison - Prisoners need to be visited above all others, as they are commonly solitary and forsaken by the rest of the world.

Then shall the righteous answer — It cannot be, that either the righteous or the wicked should answer in these very words. What we learn herefrom is, that neither of them have the same estimation of their own works as the Judge hath.
Inasmuch as ye did it to one of the least of these my brethren, ye did it to me — What encouragement is here to assist the household of faith? But let us likewise remember to do good to all men.
Depart into the everlasting fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels — Not originally for you: you are intruders into everlasting fire.
Then will they answer — So the endeavour to justify themselves, will remain with the wicked even to that day!

And these shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life everlasting — Either therefore the punishment is strictly eternal, or the reward is not: the very same expression being applied to the former as to the latter. The Judge will speak first to the righteous, in the audience of the wicked. The wicked shall then go away into everlasting fire, in the view of the righteous. Thus the damned shall see nothing of the everlasting life; but the just will see the punishment of the ungodly. It is not only particularly observable here

1. That the punishment lasts as long as the reward; but,

2. That this punishment is so far from ceasing at the end of the world, that it does not begin till then.

glossa.text: *And when.* Being about to be delivered to the cross very soon, he set before them the glory of him who triumphs, that he might make up by this promise for the scandals that were to follow. After the parables about the end of the world, the Lord now sets forth the manner of the judgment to come.

*The sheep from,* etc. There shall be two orders in the judgment, namely of the elect and of the reprobate: but of the elect some shall judge, to whom it is said: *You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the tribes of Israel.* Others shall be judged, to whom it is said: *I was hungry and you gave me to eat.* Likewise of the reprobate, some who are outside the Church shall not be judged: others who shall be judged, to whom it is said: *I was hungry, and you gave me not to eat,* etc.
*The goats.* The he-goat is a butting and rank-smelling animal, which was offered for sins in the law, and it signifies sinners: nor does he say she-goats, which can have young.

*Blessed of the Father.* Advanced by the benefit of my Father to the obtaining of glory, in which you may reign without corruption, to which you have been predestined from the foundation of the world.

*Then shall they answer.* Not distrusting the words of the Lord, but either amazed at the greatness of the king's majesty; or because every good thing that they did seems little to them, whence it is said: *The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come ((Rom. VIII))*, etc.
*Of these brethren.* My brethren and my mother are they who do the will of my Father.
*You gave me not,* etc. What does he deserve who has seized what belongs to another, if he is eternally damned who has not given anything of his own?

*Lord, when,* etc. They busy themselves to excuse themselves, as though they who were deceiving men could deceive God. But they have no excuse who would not be converted from evils and do alms; whence he adds: *As long as you did it not to one,* etc.

*Into everlasting punishment.* In vain therefore does Origen promise deliverance after many years to evil men and to the demons themselves. *Into everlasting punishment. ((AUG.))* In which matter Origen was assuredly the more merciful, who believed that the devil himself too and his angels, after punishments heavier according to their deserts and of longer duration, were to be rescued out of those torments and joined to the holy angels. But the Church has not undeservedly condemned him, both for this and for sundry other things, and chiefly for the blessednesses and miseries alternating without ceasing, and for the endless goings and returnings from those to these at fixed intervals of ages.

registers.label: Spare
lines: For everything there is a season.
And a time for every matter under heaven.
See, God is making all things new.
The old has gone; behold, the new.
Whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me.
Send us to the ones you love.
Come, let us worship at the turning of the year.
Thanks be to God. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: A year has worn down to its last hour, and you carry into this room all of it — the planting and the uprooting, the weeping and the laughing.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
Hear the One on the throne say it over your tired year: See, I am making all things new — and he wipes the tears from your face.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
He points us back out the door, toward the hungry and the stranger and the prisoner: whatever you did for them, you did for me.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
So step into the new year unafraid; the Alpha and the Omega holds both ends of your days.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us. Thanks be to God!
